extracted.intended_audience: citizens, policymakers, and readers interested in political economy, law, and social justice
extracted.subtask_short: political essay on law and plunder
extracted.subtask_description: A normative/political essay arguing what law properly is, diagnosing how law is perverted into 'legal plunder', explaining causes and consequences (currency debasement, education monopoly, suffrage issues), and prescribing the principle that law must be organised justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition_of_law_as_organized_defence
rubrics_metrics.description: The law is the collective organization of the individual right to lawful defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that Nature/God gives each person the right to defend person, liberty, and property; law is the substitution of a collective force for isolated individual forces solely to secure these rights. The collective force must have no other end than the isolated forces it replaces; it must not lawfully touch the person, liberty, or property of others. If law goes beyond this it is a perversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper_mission_of_law_protect_person_liberty_property
rubrics_metrics.description: Law's proper function is to secure persons, liberties, and properties—nothing more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When law confines itself to protecting personal safety, the freedom to labour, and security of labour's fruits, society is simple, economical, least oppressive, just, and stable. The author argues that fulfilling only this mission avoids social displacement caused by legislative interference and preserves individual responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law_must_not_be_philanthropic_or_organise_activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Law should not be used to organize or enforce provision of well-being, instruction, or moral behavior (i.e., it must not be philanthropic in scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that requiring law to extend well-being or to enforce 'fraternity' contradicts its mission and destroys liberty: legally enforcing charity, labour, commerce, education, arts, or religion encroaches on individual freedom and perverts justice. The author argues one must choose between law guaranteeing liberty/property and law mandating philanthropic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific_definition_of_plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: Plunder occurs when a portion of wealth passes from the one who acquired it, without his consent and without compensation, to one who did not create it—whether by force or artifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition is precise and not metaphorical: any uncompensated transfer of property is plunder and is what law ought to repress. If law itself effectuates such transfers, it perpetrates 'legal plunder' which is socially aggravated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification_criteria_for_legal_plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: A law is 'legal plunder' if it takes from some persons what belongs to them to give to others who did not create it, or if it performs for some what would be a crime for an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test given: 'See whether the law takes from some persons that which belongs to them, to give to others what does not belong to them.' If yes, abolish the law. Beware arguments about 'acquired rights' and sophistry used to justify legal plunder. Examples cited include slavery, protection/tariffs, perquisites, gratuities, encouragements, and gratuitous credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes_of_law_perversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Law has been perverted through two main causes: bare egotism (selfishness) and false philanthropy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-preservation and the human tendency to appropriate others' work explain plunder; because law is made by those with power, legislators may place collective force at their own service. False philanthropy explains otherwise 'benevolent' laws that redistribute by compulsion—both causes together explain systematic legal plunder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences_of_legal_plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal plunder effaces the distinction between justice and injustice, encourages reprisals, increases hatred and social discord, and tends toward social disorganisation and inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If law sanctions plunder, many will regard what is legal as necessarily just, undermining moral sense or respect for law. The text points to historical and contemporary examples (e.g., slavery and protection/tariffs in the United States) showing that legal plunder generates the gravest political conflicts and can threaten national unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three_possible_regimes_regarding_plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only three outcomes the law can produce regarding plunder: (1) partial plunder (few plunder the many), (2) universal plunder (everybody plunders everybody), or (3) absence of plunder (nobody plunders anybody).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues the correct and just goal is the absence of plunder—i.e., organising the law strictly as organised justice. Partial plunder characterises restricted elective privilege; universal plunder arises when masses legislate reprisals; absence of plunder is promoted as the principle of justice, peace, and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency_debasement_and_effects_on_prices_and_inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of false money (currency debasement or excess issuance) causes depreciation, producing a universal rise in prices that is uneven in time and effect, harming the poor more than the rich and widening inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains mechanisms: money supply changes are often linguistically misattributed to other goods; nominal coinage retains face value despite reduced real value; prices do not adjust instantaneously, allowing savvy merchants to protect themselves while labourers and small tradesmen suffer. Result: poor become poorer, social distances increase, and recovery may take centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: State_education_monopoly_is_harmful
rubrics_metrics.description: A state monopoly on education that imposes an alien historical/cultural curriculum (e.g., Roman values) misprepares youth for their own society and entrenches prejudices favouring warlike, aristocratic, or anti-labour values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because early formative years shape habits of mind, teaching youths a curriculum suited to a different social order ingrains values incompatible with the nation's needs. Therefore the urgent necessity is not for the State to 'teach' a single doctrine but to allow education—i.e., remove the monopoly of education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle_on_suffrage_responsibility_and_capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The notion of 'universal suffrage' conceals a sophism: suffrage is in practice a suffrage of those 'capable', because every vote affects the whole community and thus the community may legitimately demand some securities about the voter's capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that excluding children, women historically, or others is justified on presumed incapacity, and that the electorate does not only act for itself but for everyone. The political turmoil over suffrage would be reduced if law confined itself to its proper mission and did not create opportunities for legal plunder that tempt every class to legislate for its own profit.
